overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of Merleau-Ponty's account of the perceptual field. You'll be asked about figure–ground, horizons, motivation, perceptual constancy, and lighting as a level.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: Looking at a house from the street, you see only its front. How does Merleau-Ponty describe the house's back?

options.html: As imagined, supplied by memory of other houses
options.text: As imagined, supplied by memory of other houses
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The back isn't imagined. It's co-present as part of the house's inner horizon.

options.html: As co-present, part of the house's inner horizon
options.text: As co-present, part of the house's inner horizon
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The hidden sides aren't seen, imagined, or inferred. They're co-present as the sides you'd see if you walked around.

options.html: As inferred from the visible front by judgment
options.text: As inferred from the visible front by judgment
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Merleau-Ponty rejects the inference account. The back is co-present as part of the inner horizon.

options.html: As absent, since only the front is perceived
options.text: As absent, since only the front is perceived
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. You see a house, not a façade. The back is co-present as part of the inner horizon.

forms.stemHtml: As a friend walks toward you, her approach and her growing apparent size belong together. What relation does Merleau-Ponty call this?

options.html: Causation, since the approach produces the sensation
options.text: Causation, since the approach produces the sensation
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Merleau-Ponty sets motivation against causation. One feature makes the other appropriate without mechanically producing it.

options.html: Inference, since you conclude distance from size
options.text: Inference, since you conclude distance from size
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. You don't infer her distance. The approach and the size belong together as a relation of sense, which he calls motivation.

options.html: Motivation, a relation of sense between phenomena
options.text: Motivation, a relation of sense between phenomena
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! One perceived feature makes another appropriate, without causing it or implying it logically.

options.html: Association, since the two features often co-occur
options.text: Association, since the two features often co-occur
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Association is the empiricist principle. Merleau-Ponty calls this relation of sense motivation.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following are true of lighting, on Merleau-Ponty's account? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: It's something we see according to
options.text: It's something we see according to
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Lighting guides the gaze. We see things by it.

options.html: We adapt to it as to a level
options.text: We adapt to it as to a level
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! On entering a lit room, the lighting becomes the norm of the scene.
Correct! Once lighting is adopted as a level, colors are perceived in relation to it.

options.html: It's one more object in the field
options.text: It's one more object in the field
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Lighting isn't normally seen as an object. Looked at directly, it stops doing its work.

options.html: The brain subtracts it by inference
options.text: The brain subtracts it by inference
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's the inference account. Merleau-Ponty describes lighting as a level adopted, not an estimate subtracted.

forms.stemHtml: What is Merleau-Ponty's term for the distance and orientation at which a perceived object is given most fully, which serves as a norm toward which perception tends? Enter one word.

options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Other views of the object are lived as deviations from its optimum.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Merleau-Ponty calls this the optimum.

forms.stemHtml: Why does Merleau-Ponty say that figure–ground organization is the simplest perceptual given?

options.html: Because figures are simpler than grounds
options.text: Because figures are simpler than grounds
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The point is that even the simplest perception already has figure–ground structure.

options.html: Because the brain detects figures first
options.text: Because the brain detects figures first
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The claim is descriptive: even the simplest perception is already a figure on a ground.

options.html: Because nothing is perceived except in a field
options.text: Because nothing is perceived except in a field
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The perceptual "something" is always in the middle of something else, so perception begins organized.

options.html: Because grounds are never perceived at all
options.text: Because grounds are never perceived at all
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Grounds are perceived, as receding and shapeless. The point is that nothing is perceived outside a field.

title: The Perceptual Field
